newsitem.title: USA: Columnist asked to retract tart criticisms of D.C.
newsitem.headline: Columnist asked to retract tart criticisms of D.C.

text.p: George Will, nationally known conservative columnist for the Washington Post, is in hot water with District of Columbia activitists after saying D.C. voters got what they deserved when Congress recently took over running the city.

Known for his biting opinion pieces, the bow-tied Will wrote Thursday that D.C. has become a "national embarrassment" and suggested that voters there are "unfit for liberty" because they keep reelecting "charlatons and demagogues" like four-term Mayor Marion Barry.

But demonstrators carrying signs saying "George Will is a Media Mutant" and screaming "shame, shame George Will," circled the columnist's three-story, picket-fenced home in tony Chevy Chase, Md. on Thursday and demanded an apology.

"Mr. Will's professional colleagues should be appalled by his remarks," said Timothy Cooper, executive director of Democracy First, a group that wants full representation in the U.S. Congress for D.C. residents.
D.C. dwellers pay taxes, but they are deprived of basic political representation in Congress, said Melham, as protestors shouted "give me liberty or give me death."
Cooper added that groups will write the Washington Post next week urging it to drop Will's columns.
D.C. has one delegate to the U.S. Congress, but that person does not have a vote like the other senators and representatives from the 50 states.
A man describing himself as a friend of the Will family, came out of the house and told reporters that the columnist was "away for the weekend." This is "kind of silly," added Seth Melham.
A spokeswoman for the Post was unavailable.

Protestors are fuming over a new U.S. law that transfers Barry's authority to run critical departments like fire, public works, and human services to an emergency board set up two years ago by Congress.
The panel was convened in the wake of mounting city debts, crumbling schools and roads, and growing crime.
Will noted in Thursday's op-ed piece that one fourth of D.C. citizens have fled to the suburbs since 1970. In the meantime, Barry's municipal payroll has "swollen grotesquely," Will said.

"The mayor's office employs twice as many people as New York's mayor's office, four times as many as Boston's," Will said. Sanitation, public safety and other basic services are "collapsing," Will said.
Will noted that Barry was jailed on crack cocaine possession charges in the early 1990s.
Pointing to the writings of 19th century British political philosopher John Stuart Mill, the columnist said D.C. citizens got what they asked for.
According to Mill, citizens can render themselves "unfit" for democracy if they are careless or lazy about how they use their precious right to vote, Will said.
In such a case, a "despotic" form of government may be all they deserve, Will said tartly, citing the philosopher.
